# Why Your Service Takes Exactly 40ms Longer Than It Should

**Source:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeNTHkQgb-a/ · **Type:** Reel · **Author:** Fivenines · **Saved:** 2026-10-08

## Summary

A persistent 40ms latency penalty in production often stems from the interaction between Nagle's algorithm on the client and TCP delayed ACK on the server when requests are sent in multiple write calls. Nagle's algorithm buffers small subsequent packets waiting for an acknowledgement, while delayed ACK waits for a server response before sending an acknowledgement, causing a 40ms timer timeout on Linux. This can be resolved by enabling TCP_NODELAY on the socket or combining headers and body into a single network write.

## Caption

Daily deep dive #72: your service isn't slow. It's waiting, on purpose, for exactly 40 ms 👇

1. Symptom: 1 ms locally, 41 ms in production. Fast network, idle server, the same 40 ms every time
2. The client sends each request in two writes: headers, then body. The headers go out immediately
3. Nagle's algorithm (1984): while earlier data is unacknowledged, small packets wait in a buffer. So the body waits for an ACK
4. Delayed ACK: the server holds its ACK, hoping to piggyback it on a reply. But it can't reply without the body
5. Client waits for the ACK, server waits for data. Nothing moves until the delayed-ACK timer fires: 40 ms on Linux
6. Fix: set TCP_NODELAY on the socket (Go does this by default), or send headers and body in a single write
7. 41 ms → 1 ms
